summary: Describes how an IPv4 host can configure an address for itself automatically when no DHCP server or manual setup is available. The host picks an address from a reserved link-local range and checks that nobody else on the link uses it, which gives a usable subset of networking on a local link.

plainLanguage.summary: When nobody hands out house numbers, each house picks one for itself and asks the neighbors whether it is taken. That lets everyone on one street still find each other.

questions: automatic ip address configuration without dhcp
how does ipv4 link-local autoconfiguration work
subtitle: How an IPv4 host gives itself a 169.254/16 address, checks nobody else has it, and defends it.

tldr.problem: A host needs an IP address to talk to its neighbors, but a DHCP server or manual configuration may not be available, for example when two laptops meet on a wireless LAN.
tldr.mechanism: The host picks a pseudo-random address in 169.254/16, probes for it with ARP, announces it if nobody objects, and keeps watching for conflicts. These addresses are never forwarded by routers.
tldr.outcome: Hosts on a single link get a working, self-configured subset of IP networking without any server. The addresses only work on that link, so they suit ad hoc or isolated networks.

today: RFC 3927 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It still defines IPv4 Link-Local address configuration.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3927 describes how a host can automatically configure an interface with an IPv4 address in the 169.254/16 prefix that is valid for communication with other devices on the same physical or logical link. The prefix is registered with the IANA for this purpose. The RFC gives a motivating case: two people with IEEE 802.11 laptops who want to exchange files without setting up static addresses or a DHCP server.

These IPv4 Link-Local addresses are not suitable for devices off the link, and should only be used where stable, routable addresses are not available, such as ad hoc or isolated networks. The RFC does not recommend configuring a Link-Local address and a routable address on the same interface at once. It also says that addresses in the prefix SHOULD NOT be configured manually or by a DHCP server, because those paths skip the special duplicate-detection rules. Administrators wanting their own local addresses should use a private prefix from RFC 1918.

The specification covers IEEE 802 LANs and other link layers that support ARP, run at 1 Mbps or faster and have a round-trip latency of at most one second. It is aimed at small ad hoc networks. A host joining a link that already has 1300 hosts has a 98% chance of picking an unused address on the first try, and operators with more than 1300 hosts on one link may want to split it.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a way for devices on the same small network to name themselves when no one is in charge of handing out names. It only works inside that one small network.

sections.title: Picking an Address
sections.content:
A host picks its address with a pseudo-random number generator, uniformly in the range 169.254.1.0 to 169.254.254.255 inclusive. The first 256 and last 256 addresses of the prefix are reserved for future use and MUST NOT be chosen.

The generator MUST be arranged so that different hosts do not produce the same sequence. If the host has per-host persistent information such as its IEEE 802 MAC address, the generator SHOULD be seeded from it. That also means a host will usually pick the same address on each boot. Seeding from the real-time clock is not suitable, since hosts powered on together could then follow the same sequence and conflict forever. A host with persistent storage MAY record its chosen address and SHOULD try it first on the next boot.
sections.plainLanguage: Each device rolls dice to pick its number. The dice are rigged differently for each device, using something unique to it, so two devices do not keep picking the same numbers.

sections.title: Probing and Announcing
sections.content:
Before using a chosen address, a host MUST test whether it is already in use. It does this with an ARP Probe: a broadcast ARP Request whose sender IP address is all zeroes, so that other hosts' ARP caches are not polluted, and whose target IP address is the address being probed. The host does this whenever an interface becomes active, for example at startup, on waking from sleep or on joining a wireless network. It MUST NOT repeat the check periodically.

The host first waits a random time between zero and PROBE_WAIT (1 second), then sends PROBE_NUM (3) probes spaced randomly PROBE_MIN to PROBE_MAX (1 to 2 seconds) apart. If during this period it sees any ARP packet whose sender IP address is the probed address, or an ARP Probe for the same target address from a different hardware address, it MUST treat the address as taken and pick a new one. After more than MAX_CONFLICTS (10) conflicts it MUST limit itself to one new address per RATE_LIMIT_INTERVAL (60 seconds), to avoid ARP storms.

If nothing conflicts by ANNOUNCE_WAIT (2 seconds) after the last probe, the address is claimed. The host then MUST broadcast ANNOUNCE_NUM (2) ARP announcements, ANNOUNCE_INTERVAL (2 seconds) apart. An announcement is like a probe but with the new address in both the sender and target IP fields. It clears stale ARP cache entries left by a previous holder of the address.
sections.plainLanguage: The device shouts three times, 'Is anyone using this number?' If nobody answers, it shouts twice, 'I am using this number now!' so everyone updates their notes.

sections.title: Defending Against Conflicts
sections.content:
Conflict detection continues for as long as the address is in use. A conflicting ARP packet is any ARP request or reply whose sender IP address is the host's own address but whose sender hardware address is not that of the interface. The host MUST NOT ignore it, and MUST respond in one of two ways:

  • Immediately configure a new address.
  • If it has active TCP connections or another reason to keep the address, and has seen no other conflict within the last DEFEND_INTERVAL (10 seconds), broadcast a single ARP announcement to defend it. If a second conflict arrives within DEFEND_INTERVAL, the host MUST stop using the address and configure a new one. This stops two hosts from defending the same address in an endless loop.

Before abandoning an address, a host SHOULD try to reset existing connections that use it. All ARP packets, replies included, that carry a Link-Local sender IP address MUST be sent by link-layer broadcast, so that conflicting hosts see each other. Hosts SHOULD NOT send periodic gratuitous ARPs to find conflicts sooner. Section 4 explains that when two separate links are joined, the broadcast replies let the clashing hosts discover the conflict exactly when someone tries to communicate.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone else says they own your number, you can either pick a new one right away or say once, 'No, this one is mine.' If they challenge you again soon after, you give in and pick a new number.

sections.title: Forwarding Rules
sections.content:
If a destination is in 169.254/16 (excluding 169.254.255.255, the broadcast address for the prefix), the sender MUST ARP for it and send the packet directly on the local link, whether the interface has a Link-Local or routable address. A host MUST NOT send a packet with a Link-Local destination to a router. If the destination is outside the prefix, the host SHOULD use a routable source address if it can. If it must use a Link-Local source, it still MUST ARP for the destination and send directly, which the RFC paraphrases as 'ARP for everything'.

Packets whose source or destination is in the prefix MUST NOT be forwarded by any network device, regardless of TTL, and this applies to multicast too. A sensible default for applications sending from a Link-Local address is to set the IPv4 TTL to 1. The prefix MUST NOT be subnetted, because ARP-based conflict detection relies on broadcasts that subnets would not carry. Routers MUST NOT forward such packets and MUST NOT indiscriminately answer ARP requests for addresses in the prefix. The RFC also says Link-Local addresses MUST NOT be stored in the DNS, and DNS clients MUST NOT send queries for names under 254.169.in-addr.arpa..
sections.plainLanguage: Messages for these numbers never leave the street. A device does not give them to the post office, it hands them straight to the neighbor.

sections.title: Living With DHCP, Routable Addresses and Several Interfaces
sections.content:
A host SHOULD NOT hold both an operable routable address and a Link-Local address on one interface, though both MAY exist during a transition. Link-Local assignment depends solely on the interface state, and a host MUST NOT alter its DHCP behavior just because it assigned a Link-Local address. When a routable address becomes operable, the host MUST use it for new communications and cease advertising the Link-Local one, while it SHOULD continue existing conversations on the old address. The RFC adds that early implementations modified the DHCP state machine, and field experience showed this reduced DHCP reliability.

Hosts with several interfaces face unresolved problems, which the RFC lists but does not solve: scoped addresses, ambiguity when the same Link-Local destination can be resolved on more than one link, and routing to non-Link-Local hosts. It also warns about the 'autoimmune response', where two interfaces on one link defend against each other, and suggests running the algorithm independently per interface. Applications may also fail when addresses change, so vendors SHOULD expose address-change events and Link-Local addresses MUST NOT be forwarded to off-link destinations through an application protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Having a street number and a city address at once can confuse people, so a device prefers the proper address whenever it gets one. The special street number is just a fallback.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Configuring an address may expose a host to IP-based attacks that it was not open to before. ARP is insecure: a malicious host can answer every ARP request with its own hardware address and so claim every address on the link. Local links such as wireless LANs offer no physical security, so implementers must not assume a local-only device can skip normal security measures.

The claim-and-defend design adds its own weakness. An on-link attacker can send ARP packets that force a host to switch address and break its connections, steer which addresses it picks, or stop it from ever finishing address selection. A node that gives up an address also leaves existing TCP connections open to hijack, which is why hosts SHOULD try to reset them first. Section 2.10 adds a privacy note: addresses derived from a hash of the MAC address could be linked to a person, which is a reason to keep them from leaving the link.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone on the same street can lie and say they own your number, so you cannot fully trust neighbors. Being on a small network does not make a device safe.

sections.title: Timing Constants
sections.content: Section 9 lists the timing constants of the protocol and says they are not intended to be user configurable. Links that run below 1 Mbps or above one second of latency may need different values for the probe and announcement counts and intervals, the rate limit, and DEFEND_INTERVAL. The IANA allocated the prefix 169.254/16 and handles the first and last 256 addresses by Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: The waiting times and the number of shouts are fixed, so every device behaves in the same way.

messages.label: ARP Probe (3 times)
messages.note: Broadcast, all-zero sender IP, target is the chosen address.

messages.label: ARP announcement (2 times)
messages.note: Sent after no conflict; sender and target are the new address.
